output.title: ICC says Duterte 'shall continue to be detained' | ABS-CBN News
output.description: The International Criminal Court (ICC) on Wednesday said former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte "shall continue to be detained," as there have been no nota
output.text: Former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte appears at the International Criminal Court during the third status conference in the case of The Prosecutor v. Rodrigo Roa Duterte, September 16, 2026. Handout/ICC via Flickr THE HAGUE, Netherlands ( UPDATED ) — The International Criminal Court (ICC) on Wednesday said former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte " shall continue to be detained ," citing an increased risk that he could flee or interfere with witnesses and court proceedings. In a 5-page decision signed by Trial Chamber III Presiding Judge Joanna Korner, the Chamber also found no significant change in circumstances that would warrant Duterte's release or alter the previous finding that he could commit the same crimes. The ICC's Trial Chamber III had released its second decision on the review of Duterte's detention after the third status conference on his case, where the former Philippine leader made an in-person appearance. READ: Rodrigo Duterte makes first in-person appearance at ICC In its decision, the ICC noted that the Chamber "shall review and modify the initial decision on detention 'if it is satisfied that changed circumstances so require'." In reviewing the developments after its first decision on the review of Duterte's detention , the Chamber noted that there is "a likelihood of the Accused absconding and/or obstructing or endangering the investigation or the court proceedings." With the prosecution having submitted its Witness and Evidence Lists, the Chamber also noted that this "increases the Accused's ability to interfere with witnesses, either directly or through his family or supporters in the Philippines." Duterte's defense team said on Tuesday that the former president is suffering from severe memory loss, sometimes forgetting his lawyer's name. READ: Former president Duterte suffering from 'significant memory impairment' — defense But with regards to his fitness, the Chamber said that "the Defense's Observations do not provide any information that constitutes new facts or a change in circumstances." "The Chamber... finds no notable change in circumstances that warrant the release of the Accused, with or without conditions," they said. "For these reasons, the Chamber hereby decides that the Accused shall continue to be detained." Duterte faces three counts of crimes against humanity, with prosecutors alleging his involvement in at least 76 murders between 2013 and 2018 during his offensive against drug users and sellers. His trial is scheduled to start on November 30. He is the first Asian former head of state to face trial at the ICC, which prosecutes individuals for the world's worst crimes such as war crimes and crimes against humanity. — Prosecution, victims oppose release — The decision followed submissions from the parties on the periodic review of Duterte's continued detention. In separate filings dated September 14, the prosecution and the Common Legal Representatives of Victims (CLRV) of the former Philippine president's war on drugs opposed any modification to Duterte's detention, while the defense argued that the issue of his fitness to stand trial should first be resolved. In its 5-page submission, the prosecution said continued detention remains necessary because the circumstances that warranted Duterte's detention have not changed. It also argued that the risk of flight has increased for the 81-year-old former president, particularly with the trial date now set and the prosecution's addition of eight incidents to the charges, which it said increased the prospect of a lengthy prison sentence. On the risk to witnesses, the prosecution said: "The question of the risks to witnesses 'revolves around the possibility, not the inevitability, of a 'future occurrence'. Mr Duterte's history shows that he is able and has the means, either directly or through his associates, to interfere with [REDACTED]," the filing read. The prosecution therefore argued that Duterte's "continued detention is necessary to ensure he does not interfere with witnesses." Meanwhile, the CLRV opposed any modification of Duterte's detention, arguing that the legal grounds for keeping him in custody remain unchanged. The victims' representatives said the factors previously considered by the ICC—including the alleged risk of flight, the gravity of the charges, and Duterte's continued access to networks of supporters and influence—remain applicable. They also said many victims and witnesses continue to fear possible retaliation, intimidation or interference if Duterte is released. The victims' representatives maintained that detention remains necessary to protect the integrity of the proceedings and ensure Duterte's appearance at trial. — Defense wants fitness issue resolved first — The defense, led by British barrister Peter Haynes, did not seek Duterte's immediate release. Instead, it argued that the detention issue cannot be fully assessed until the ICC rules on whether Duterte is fit to stand trial. The defense said that if Duterte is found unfit and the proceedings are adjourned, this could constitute a material change in circumstances that would affect the basis for his continued detention. The defense said it intends to revisit the detention issue after the court rules on his fitness to stand trial. The defense also noted that it had requested a medical examination in May 2026 to determine whether Duterte remains capable of meaningfully participating in the proceedings. Expert reports have since been completed, and submissions on their findings have been filed. However, the Chamber has yet to issue a ruling on Duterte's fitness to stand trial. The defense argued that the Expert Panel's findings were inconclusive and disputed. It also sought further examination by a neurologist and asked that the parties be allowed to question the appointed experts, "either orally or in writing, on the findings and conclusions set out in their reports" before the court makes a final determination. The Trial Chamber said the fitness issue remains pending. However, it found that the medical reports and the defense's submissions did not provide grounds to modify Duterte's detention. — with Agence France-Presse RELATED VIDEO: Former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte appears at the International Criminal Court during the third status conference in the case of The Prosecutor v. Rodrigo Roa Duterte, September 16, 2026. Handout/ICC via Flickr THE HAGUE, Netherlands ( 4th UPDATE ) — Former Philippines president Rodrigo Duterte appeared in person at the International Criminal Court for the first time Wednesday, as he faces charges over his "war on drugs" that killed thousands. The 81-year-old had appeared by video link when he was first brought to the court in The Hague, but had since skipped hearings, with his defense team saying he was too ill. READ: Former president Duterte suffering from 'significant memory impairment' — defense Dressed in a dark suit and white shirt with no tie, the former president sat with his chin resting on his hands as proceedings opened. Judge Joanna Korner noted his appearance in court for the first time, and said he could leave the court at any time without seeking permission from the bench. But he stayed throughout the hearing, which lasted one hour and 15 minutes, showing no emotion and seeming to follow proceedings through headphones. His grandchildren, Omar and Isabelle Duterte, were among those seated in the front row of the gallery. After the hearing, Duterte's lawyers pointed him toward the gallery, where his grandchildren and supporters were seated. He waved and smiled at them, and his grandchildren waved back. Omar later said he was unsure whether his grandfather could see them clearly from behind the glass as they waved to each other. The two grandchildren arrived in The Hague on Monday for their scheduled family visits. Duterte's supporters in the gallery said they were happy to see him in person but also saddened that he remains detained. He is the first Asian former head of state to face trial at the ICC, which prosecutes individuals for the world's worst crimes such as war crimes and crimes against humanity. Duterte faces three counts of crimes against humanity, with prosecutors alleging his involvement in at least 76 murders between 2013 and 2018 during his offensive against drug users and sellers. Korner has set November 30 as the start date of the trial, which could take months or even years. The only time Duterte had been seen since his arrest in March 2025 was an initial appearance via video, where he seemed confused and tired, his speech barely audible. - 'It's impossible' - Former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte appears at the International Criminal Court during the third status conference in the case of The Prosecutor v. Rodrigo Roa Duterte, September 16, 2026. Handout/ICC via Flickr Wednesday's hearing was a "status hearing" for the parties and the judge to fix logistical details. Lawyers clashed over evidence filed by the prosecution, which they said was around 15,000 pieces but the defense put at more than 62,000 documents. "It's quite enormous. It's impossible," said defense lawyer Peter Haynes. "We haven't got a prayer of reading" such a mountain of documents before the trial starts, said Haynes. "The current state of the case is a mess. If I had a younger, healthier client, I would invite you to put back the trial by six months... but I don't," said Duterte's lawyer. Korner chided the prosecution for "wholesale dumping" of documents and urged the parties to work together to reduce the size of the case file. Relatives of some of those killed in the anti-drugs campaign welcomed Duterte's appearance in court. Randy Delos Santos, 48, an uncle of Kian Delos Santos, a teenager killed by police in August 2017, when Duterte was president, told AFP: "Of course, we are very happy that he is now able to attend in person. READ: Victims urge ICC to keep Rodrigo Duterte behind bars before trial "We hope that his being physically fit will help speed up the hearings," Santos told AFP in Manila. In a submission published Tuesday, Duterte's lawyers said he suffered from "significant memory impairment that prevents him from retaining recent information and reliably accessing memories". Judges are weighing whether he is mentally fit to be tried and have ordered a medical assessment by three experts. That assessment has not been made public but Duterte's defense cited the results of examinations contained in the report. According to the defense, these examination showed Duterte thinks he is living in 2007 or 2008, that he is 84 or 85 years old, and could not recall the name of the current US president. - 'Bluster and hyperbole' - During hearings in February, the prosecution alleged Duterte killed thousands of suspected drug dealers and users, first as mayor of Davao City, then as president. The true number of killings during his campaign in the Philippines is thought to be in the thousands, and lawyers for the victims have argued that a full trial could encourage more families to come forward. His then defense lawyer Nicolas Kaufman told the court in February his client "absolutely" maintained his innocence. Kaufman told ICC judges the evidence against Duterte was "wholly insufficient" and the charges "grievously misplaced and politically motivated". He argued that while Duterte used "bluster and hyperbole" in his speeches, he also frequently ordered authorities only to shoot in self-defense. Duterte remains popular in the Philippines, where many favored his tough approach to crime. — with a report from Jofelle Tesorio, ABS-CBN News WATCH: A protester holds a life-size cartboard cutouts of former Philippines' president Rodrigo Duterte during a demonstration in his support outside the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague on February 23, 2026. Simon Wohlfahrt, AFP/File MANILA — The list of evidence in the trial of former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte became a topic of a lengthy discussion during the third status conference for his crimes against humanities case at the International Criminal Court on Wednesday. Presiding Judge Joanna Korner first raised the issue about more than 15,000 items for exhibits. She reiterated that the Chamber wants to avoid the wholesale dumping of exhibits, evidence and videos that are repetitive or have limited relevance. Senior trial lawyer Julian Nicholls explained that a big part of that number involves a large data set that they did not disclose publicly but in a private session. He did say later that the data set involves information from the Philippine National Police on the total of deaths in the Duterte administration’s anti-drug campaign. Rodrigo Duterte makes first in-person appearance at ICC “This data set provides a kind of bottom number of what the government, and the Philippines’ national police say, are war on drugs numbers, where a suspect was killed in a police operation, and that comes around 3,420 deaths that they said occured in that period nationwide,” he explained. “The data set was truly enormous and when it came, it was in an absolute mess when we received it,” he also said, adding that their team spent hours organizing the data set. Nicholls also said they were not dumping it in court but they are trying to fix the information they have for the trial and they will still try to streamline and cut it even more. “We may have gotten broad. We’ll try to narrow it down,” he said. The Chamber then requested a list of key items to be presented. “[I]f a number of them say the same thing, we would expect you to select the best, the Defense will obviously have access to all these documents,” Korner said. She said the prosecution will not have to include "every single document", just “those that are most capable of proving what you wish to establish.” The list is to be submitted at least seven days ahead of the next status conference. The defense, led by Peter Haynes, decried the tons of evidence they had to go through. He said the more than 15,000 exhibits that were mentioned were just non-witness exhibits. There are still more than 3,000 witness items. “So not withstanding your imploring them to be focused and economical in May, the list of exhibits has quadrupled,” he said. Haynes said the prosecution had exhibits since November 2021 and the defense was only told about them in July. They also complained about missing pages, multiple disclosures of the same document and misidentification A solution he proposed was to direct opening of a new case file with a new exhibit list. “I would invite you to consider migrating a smaller case to a new case file, and perhaps limiting the overall disclosure therein to about 10,000 documents,” he also said. According to Haynes, he could have asked the Chamber to push back the trial for another six months if only he had a younger and healthier client. “It’s the only solution we can suggest given the state of the case, which is a mess," he said. Korner gave the defense seven days to file a motion but said she believes this has to be resolved quickly and without the court’s intervention as much as possible. “If you could put down what your complaints are, and any suggestions…if you could do that. And Mr. Nicholls, if you could respond,” she said. “But I would encourage, however, the parties to again get together about this. If it can be resolved amicably without involving the chamber then that would be very helpful,” Korner added. Wednesday's hearing was a "status hearing" for the parties and the judge to fix logistical details. It also marked Duterte’s first in person appearance at the ICC in a year since his arrest. Meanwhile, the Duterte Panagutin Network Netherlands, which earlier held a rally outside the ICC, said Duterte's appearance in court showed that he was capable of facing the proceedings. "Duterte's appearance in court today proves he has been feigning sick all this time. It was all a delaying tactic, delaying justice and delaying healing for the victims’ families. We sincerely hope to see him again on the first day of the trial on November 30th, and for him to finally face the victims of his crimes," said Fiona Magallanes, Bayan Netherlands and convenor of Panagutin Network NL. "Duterte has now appeared in court and looks well, exposing the myth that his camp has continuously pushed of a sickly old man supposedly unfit to stand trial." The group said it hopes to see Duterte again when the trial formally begins. Duterte faces three counts of crimes against humanity, with prosecutors alleging his involvement in at least 76 murders between 2013 and 2018 during his offensive against drug users and sellers. Simon Wohlfahrt, AFP/File Legal representatives for victims in the case against Rodrigo Duterte are strongly pressing the International Criminal Court to maintain his detention, arguing that the former Philippine leader continues to pose a flight risk and a threat to witnesses. This, after Duterte’s defense team said the former president is suffering from severe memory loss and sometimes forgets his lawyer's name. The 81-year-old Duterte faces charges of crimes against humanity at the ICC over his so-called "war on drugs" during which thousands were killed, according to prosecutors. His trial is scheduled to start on November 30, but judges are weighing whether he is mentally fit to be tried and ordered a medical assessment by three experts. That assessment has not been made public but Duterte's defense and the ICC prosecutor reacted to it in documents dated September 14 but published on the ICC website on Tuesday. Lead Counsel Peter Haynes, KC, argued that independent medical assessments paint a clear picture of an accused suffering from "significant memory impairment that prevents him from retaining recent information and reliably accessing memories." According to the filing, the panel of experts appointed by the Trial Chamber to evaluate Mr. Duterte found that his cognitive hurdles make it difficult for him to engage with the charges or give proper instructions to his legal team. The defense noted that Mr. Duterte remembers his lead counsel's name "only sometimes." WHAT MEDICAL EXPERTS FOUND Despite documenting low test scores indicative of moderate to severe cognitive impairment, the expert panel concluded that Mr. Duterte possessed the necessary capacities to stand trial, attributing his poor testing results to "underperformance" or a lack of motivation rather than a definitive neurological disorder. The defense sharply contested this conclusion, pointing out that the experts' own findings failed to rule out an underlying neurological condition. “The probability of the latter hypothesis is not a mere suggestion advanced by the Defence, but a plausible explanation put forward by two out of the three appointed experts. Professor [REDACTED] expressly made clear that his reference to underperformance was valid only “in the absence” of any neurological disorders. 23 A scenario that, unlike in his December 2025 report, 24 he now appears unwilling to discount, by stating that “[REDACTED]” cannot be ruled out,” as explained in the document. The filing emphasized that the actual cause of Mr. Duterte's testing failures "remains unknown," noting that the appointed neurologist omitted straight forward ancillary examinations that could have provided a clear diagnosis without requiring the patient's cooperation. “Further examinations which did not require the patient’s cooperation – [REDACTED] – were available and would have been able to clarify this question, yet were not performed.” "The Defence does not seek to supplant the Professors' expertise," the legal team stated, urging strict adherence to instructions and the exhaustion of all available medical examinations to provide judges with a robust evidentiary basis. ‘DUTERTE THINKS HE IS LIVING IN 2007-2008’ The defense observations detailed multiple instances during medical interviews where Mr. Duterte struggled with fundamental orientation. The filing stated that Mr. Duterte could not remember being examined by the panel ten months prior, remained incapable of placing himself in time and space—believing he is living in 2007 or 2008—and failed to correctly identify members of his own family, including his grandchildren. Furthermore, he believed his last election took place 46 years ago and that he is 84 or 85 years old, the defense argued. The legal team argued that these consistent memory lapses make it impossible for counsel to place confidence in information provided about past events or to adequately prepare a defense against tens of thousands of disclosed items of evidence, hundreds of hours of video footage, and voluminous transcripts. Acting Prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang, meanwhile, urged the judges to rule that the former leader possesses the capacity required to understand the proceedings, follow the evidence, and instruct his legal counsel. “Pursuant to Trial Chamber Ill’s (the “Chamber”) decisions… the Prosecution provides its observations on the Panel of Experts’ joint and individual reports… Understand the charges… Instruct counsel in the preparation and conduct of his defence,” Niang said in observations submitted to Trial Chamber III on September 14, 2026. The prosecution's position centers squarely on the unanimous findings of a specially appointed panel of multidisciplinary medical experts. FIT FOR TRIAL According to the filing, the experts conducted in-person interviews, examinations, and assessments of Mr. Duterte after reviewing relevant medical records and consulting clinicians and custody staff. The prosecution said the experts found "[REDACTED]" in his condition since their initial assessments more than six months prior. Instead, the evaluation indicates that the former president is fit for trial and capable of "meaningfully exercising his procedural and fair trial rights." The panel was initially formed following a defense request in May 2026 for a medical evaluation. Both the prosecution and defense supported the re-appointment of the experts who evaluated the accused during pre-trial proceedings. Addressing the evaluation process, the prosecution noted that the panel members maintained strict independence, providing a formal declaration confirming the absence of any conflicts of interest. The filing also points out that certain expert observations suggested instances of "reduced effort and unreliability during assessments," noting behavioral notes such as a "[REDACTED]" in a "[REDACTED]" environment. With the medical findings clear and the panel in full agreement on its methodology and conclusions, the prosecution argues that holding a dedicated hearing on Mr. Duterte's fitness is unnecessary. Under the court's regulatory framework, such a hearing is discretionary rather than mandatory. "There is no statutory requirement to hold a hearing on fitness to stand trial in the Court’s regulatory framework, nor is one envisioned within the process under rule 135 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence," the prosecution stated in the document. To accommodate the former leader during court proceedings, the expert panel outlined several practical adjustments. “Pursuant to the Chamber’s instructions,30 the Panel provided a number of practical suggestions, including those aimed at facilitating Mr Duterte’s effective participation at trial.” The prosecution defers to the court registry regarding the feasibility of these measures, though it noted that schedule adjustments might occasionally need flexibility to accommodate incoming witness testimonies. “The Prosecution considers that the above-mentioned measures proposed by the Panel are reasonable and defers to the Registry in relation to the feasibility of their practical implementation, as well as to the Chamber’s discretion in their adoption. In relation specifically to the proposal to commence hearings [REDACTED], the Prosecution flags that exceptions may need to be made in order to accommodate witness testimony [REDACTED].” Furthermore, the prosecution contends that a continuous cycle of medical reassessments is unnecessary. It noted that rule provisions for ongoing reviews apply strictly to situations where an accused individual has been found unfit. “There is no ongoing statutory obligation on Chambers to reassess an accused’s fitness, as rule 135(4) applies only in situations where an accused is found to be unfit to stand trial.” 'A MATTER OF LAW RATHER THAN SCIENCE' In its observations, the defense invoked Rule 135 and underscored that it is ultimately for the Trial Chamber—as a matter of law rather than science—to determine fitness to stand trial to ensure fair proceedings. “Pursuant to Rule 135, a Chamber may order a medical examination… Accordingly, it is for the Chamber alone to determine this question – as it is a matter of law rather than science.” The defense has formally requested the Trial Chamber to direct the appointed neurologist to complete all necessary ancillary examinations to establish a formal diagnosis regarding any neurological condition. In the alternative, the defense asked the court to permit the parties to question the experts either orally or in writing to resolve inconsistencies in their reports before any trial proceedings move forward. VICTIMS SPEAK OUT In a public redacted filing submitted to Trial Chamber III on September 15, the Common Legal Representatives of Victims maintained that the foundational factors requiring Duterte's custody remain entirely unchanged. The legal team stressed that keeping him detained at the seat of the Court in The Hague is the sole mechanism capable of guaranteeing his physical presence at trial and preventing any potential interference with the judicial process. "Victims expect to finally see Mr Duterte appear in person in the courtroom," the legal representatives stated in the document. They added that continued detention is vital "to prevent any risk that victims and witnesses may be subjected, directly or indirectly, to intimidation, threats, interference, or other forms of undue influence that could undermine their participation in the proceedings and the proper administration of justice." Duterte was surrendered to the Hague by the Philippine government on March 12, 2025, following an arrest warrant issued by Pre-Trial Chamber I. Under the rules of the Rome Statute, his detention is subjected to periodic reviews at least every 120 days. Following the confirmation of charges against him on April 23, 2026, the Chamber previously ruled that the milestone increased the risk of flight, necessitating his continued imprisonment. The latest filing also addresses ongoing discussions surrounding Duterte's health and his fitness to stand trial. While the Defence has repeatedly argued that medical conditions should warrant interim release, the victims' legal team noted that independent medical evaluations by a court-appointed multidisciplinary panel of experts have not altered the legal landscape. “The Defence’s argument that Mr Duterte’s health conditions supported interim release rather than continued detention… the independent medical expertise does not affect the prior judicial determination that Mr Duterte continues to pose a significant flight risk,” said in the document. The Chamber previously emphasized that fitness to stand trial hinges on whether an accused can effectively exercise fair trial rights rather than the mere presence of medical conditions. “Emphasising that “the question of whether an accused is fit to stand trial does not depend, in and of itself, on whether he or she has particular medical conditions, but whether he or she is able to effectively exercise his or her fair trial rights in the proceedings.” According to the victims' representatives, “it is nevertheless important to emphasize, for the purposes of the present observations, that the independent medical expertise does not affect the prior judicial determination that Mr Duterte continues to pose a significant flight risk.” They pointed out that the gravity of the charges, the potential sentence, and Duterte’s longstanding public posture toward the Court and its legitimacy remain unchanged. For many affected individuals and their families, the proceedings represent a vital avenue for accountability. “Victims and their families attach considerable importance to these proceedings, viewing them as the only avenue to obtain justice.” However, the legal filing highlights that deep-seated fears persist within local communities. "Many continue to fear threats, retaliation and stigmatisation in the communities due to Mr Duterte’s continuing influence," the representatives noted, emphasizing that the protection of participants can only be effectively ensured through continued custody. This makes it impossible for him to engage with the case "let alone give proper instructions to his Lead Counsel, whose name he only sometimes remembers", said his chief defense lawyer, Peter Haynes. Haynes said he was being forced to prepare the case without meaningful input from his client. The prosecution, in its own heavily redacted seven-page submission, concluded Duterte was "capable of meaningfully exercising his procedural and fair trial rights, and that he is fit for trial". However, the experts were unable to determine whether Duterte's results stemmed from "malingering or a lack of motivation" or "a genuine inability to... complete the tests as a consequence of an underlying neurological condition", said the defense. output.title: Rodrigo Duterte to remain detained — ICC trial chamber
output.description: The International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III has unanimously decided to keep former President Rodrigo Duterte detained.
output.text:
THE HAGUE – The International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III has unanimously decided to keep former President Rodrigo Duterte detained.

In a decision released shortly after the conclusion of the third status conference, the Chamber found a likelihood of Duterte “absconding and/or obstructing or endangering the investigation or the court proceedings.”

“In respect of the latter considerations, owing to the Prosecution’s submission of the Witness and Evidence Lists, (thereby disclosing the identities of the witnesses and the contents of their expected testimony), this increases the Accused’s ability to interfere with witnesses, either directly or through his family or supporters in the Philippines,” the decision read.

The Chamber noted it has yet to decide on the issue of Duterte’s fitness, as the defense’s requested “greater medical certainty” while challenging the expert panel’s report.

However, the Chamber said the observations of Duterte’s lawyers “do not provide any information that constitutes new facts or a change in circumstances” which would warrant a modification of his detention.

The ICC Office of the Prosecutor is asking the Trial Chamber III to order the continued detention of Duterte, noting that it is “necessary” so he would not “interfere with witnesses.”

Acting Prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang said “there has been no change” in Duterte’s circumstances that would prompt the Trial Chamber III to revise its previous order on the former president’s detention.

“To the contrary,” Niang noted in an observation filed on September 14, “there have been changes in circumstances that have increased the risk Mr. Duterte presents under articles 58(1)(b)(i) and (ii) of the Statute.”

Niang was referring to the Rome Statute’s article on issuing a warrant of arrest, ensuring the appearance at a trial of a person facing charges, and that such person “does not obstruct or endanger the investigation or the court proceedings.”

Meanwhile, Duterte attended, for the first time this Wednesday, September 16, 2026, the ICC's status conference in his crimes against humanity case.

According to GMA stringer Andy Peñafuerte III, the former official was already seated when the judges arrived.

Unlike the previous two hearings, Duterte did not waive his appearance.

“This is the first time that Mr. Duterte has been in this court. As far as the trial chamber is concerned, if he wishes to leave for any reason, he may do so,” Presiding Judge Joanna Korner said.

Duterte’s trial is scheduled to begin on November 30.

He is facing crimes against humanity charges over alleged killings during his time as President and Davao City mayor.

output.title: ICC chamber orders continued detention of Rodrigo Duterte
output.description: Former President Rodrigo Duterte will continue to be detained in The Hague pending the start of his trial for alleged crimes against humanity, the International Criminal Court (ICC) said Friday.
output.text:
Former President Rodrigo Duterte will continue to be detained in The Hague pending the start of his trial for alleged crimes against humanity, the International Criminal Court (ICC) said Friday.

In its decision, the ICC Trial Chamber III said the defense's and the ICC Registry's observations on Duterte's health condition "do not present information that constitute new facts or a change in circumstances in comparison to the information" submitted by the Court-appointed medical experts.

It also cited Duterte's refusal to recognize the jurisdiction of the ICC over him.

"Such statement demonstrates at its lowest that the accused will not comply with any orders that might be made in respect of a release from custody," the Court said.

"Taken together with his access to vast resources and contacts, including his family and supporters in the Philippines who may assist him in evading justice, the Chamber finds that, notwithstanding the defense's submissions regarding the accused’s health condition, there is a real and substantial risk that the accused could nonetheless abscond or obstruct justice either on his own or through his associates," it added.

"Consequently, the Chamber finds that the accused’s physical condition and cognitive capacities referred to by the defense do not constitute factors which outweigh the risks outlined above."

Earlier, the ICC Registry said that the 81-year-old Duterte is under cell monitoring due to his status as an elderly detained person with increased fall risk because of age and several chronic physical ailments.

On January 26, the Pre-Trial Chamber I ruled Duterte was fit to take part in the confirmation of charges hearings in February while in detention. This decision was upheld by the Appeals Chamber on March 6.

"Pursuant to Article 60(3) of the [Rome] Statute, the Chamber shall review the initial decision on release or detention rendered following a request for interim release under Article 60(2) of the Statute. Rule 118(2) of the Rules requires the Chamber to do so at least every 120 days," the Trial Chamber III said.

Duterte allowed to skip status conference

Meanwhile, the Court granted the defense's request for Duterte to skip the first status conference scheduled for May 27.

The defense was given until Monday, May 25, to submit Duterte's signed written request.

Among the topics to be discussed by the parties during the conference are the commencement date of the trial and deadlines leading up to trial, anticipated evidence, agreed facts, and the languages to be used.

"The status conference will be public. However, in order to avoid disclosure of sensitive information regarding witness protection and security issues, the Chamber may order the use of private sessions," the Trial Chamber III said.

The Pre-Trial Chamber I on April 23 confirmed the charges of crimes against humanity against Duterte in connection with the killings in his war on drugs when he was mayor of Davao City and president.

The decision to confirm the charges came a day after the Appeals Chamber denied Duterte's appeal of the Court's jurisdiction over his case. —VBL GMA News

output.title: ICC: Duterte to stay detained
output.description: Former president Rodrigo Duterte will remain in detention in The Hague ahead of his trial for crimes against humanity before the International Criminal Court, judges ruled on Friday.
output.text: MANILA, Philippines — Former president Rodrigo Duterte will remain in detention in The Hague ahead of his trial for crimes against humanity before the International Criminal Court (ICC), judges ruled on Friday. In an eight-page decision dated May 22, the ICC Trial Chamber III said there was no notable change in circumstance that would justify Duterte’s release, either with or without conditions. The judges stressed that the recent confirmation of charges against Duterte even “increases the risk that an accused may abscond and is therefore not a change in circumstances that militates in favor of conditional release, but rather one supporting continued detention.” They said Duterte’s refusal to attend his confirmation hearing in February and his statement that he does not recognize the jurisdiction of the ICC, “demonstrates at its lowest that the Accused will not comply with any orders that might be made in respect of a release from custody.” “Taken together with his access to vast resources and contacts, including his family and supporters in the Philippines who may assist him in evading justice, the chamber finds that… there is a real and substantial risk that the Accused could nonetheless abscond or obstruct justice either on his own or through his associates,” read the eight-page decision. The trial chamber also rejected arguments from Duterte’s camp that his supposed deteriorating health condition justified his release. Nicholas Kaufman, Duterte’s former defense counsel, earlier argued that the former president’s physical condition constituted a change in circumstance that could warrant conditional release. However, the judges pointed to findings by court-appointed medical experts, saying their reports “do not contain any information that warrants modifying the Accused’s detention.” “The Chamber further observes that the defense’s and the registry’s observations do not present information that constitute new facts or a change in circumstances in comparison to the information provided in the panel’s reports,” the judges added. A law expert from the University of the Philippines College of Law welcomed the ICC ruling, saying it was consistent with the tribunal’s handling of detention cases. “The ICC decision not to allow his release and that he will remain in detention is actually in line with the ICC’s decision on other accused in their detention centers. There is indeed a possibility that former president Rodrigo Duterte will become a flight risk… The evasion of arrest by Sen. dela Rosa is another factual circumstance that perhaps in the eyes of the international community there is an active effort to evade any process for international accountability,” UP College of Law senior lecturer and ICC assistant to counsel Ross Tugade said in an interview with dzMM. “We welcome at least the decision to have him remain in detention because the ultimate goal, at least for us, (is to) really see the progress of the process before the ICC,” Tugade added. Meanwhile, in a separate order, the trial judges allowed Duterte to skip his case’s first status conference scheduled on May 27. Duterte’s defense team earlier filed the request, saying that the mandatory obligation for an accused to be present at trial does not apply to other hearings such as status conferences that are “essentially administrative in nature.” “The Chamber authorizes the request and orders the defense to file on the record a signed waiver by the Accused, bearing in mind the requirements provided for in the statutory framework,” the judges said. — Bella Cariaso Philstar.com is one of the most vibrant, opinionated, discerning communities of readers on cyberspace. output.text: MANILA, Philippines — Former president Rodrigo Duterte will remain in detention in The Hague after trial judges of the International Criminal Court (ICC) found “no notable change” in circumstances that would war- rant his release. The decision on Duterte’s second review detention was released by the ICC Trial Chamber III hours after he appeared for the first time in person before the international tribunal. “The chamber finds that the prospect of the accused facing a trial, and (in the event of a conviction), a lengthy prison sentence , has increased. There is therefore, a likelihood of the accused absconding and/or obstructing or endangering the investigation or the court proceedings,” the five-page decision stated. “In respect of the latter considerations, owing to the prosecution’s submission of the witness and evidence lists, (thereby disclosing the identities of the witnesses and the contents of their expected testimony), this increases his ability to interfere with witnesses, either directly or through his family or supporters in the Philippines,” it added. Although the decision on Duterte’s fitness to stand trial is still pending, the judges also ruled that the expert panel’s reports “do not contain any new information that warrants a modification of the detention.” Duterte, 81, appeared subdued as he sat in the last row of the defense section during the third status conference on the crimes against humanity case filed against him before the tribunal. Sporting a different hairstyle and dressed in a black suit and white shirt, the former president mainly listened as the parties discussed details of his upcoming trial, currently scheduled to begin on Nov. 30. ICC Trial Chamber III Presiding Judge Joanna Korner did not directly address Duterte, but his presence was noted at the start of proceedings. Duterte has been detained at the ICC in The Hague since his arrest. He was last seen by the public during his initial appearance hearing on March 14, 2025. His defense team previously argued that he is no longer fit to stand trial, citing his supposed deteriorating medical condition. But in a statement, the Duterte Panagutin Network said his appearance at the ICC is proof that the trial can proceed. “Duterte has now appeared in court and looks well, exposing the myth that his camp has continuously pushed of a sickly old man that was supposedly ‘unfit to stand trial,’” said Fiona Magallanes, convenor of Panagutin Netherlands, a part of the network pushing for accountability over drug war killings. “Duterte’s appearance in court today proves that he has been feigning sick all this time. It was a delaying tactic, delaying justice and delaying healing for the victims’ families. We sincerely hope to see him again on the first day of the trial on Nov. 30, and for him to finally face the victims of his crimes,” she added. Korner said Trial Chamber III will soon make a ruling on Duterte’s fitness to stand trial, based on the reports of medical experts tapped to conduct an independent assessment of his condition. The status conference focused on details of the prosecution’s case, including its list of witnesses and evidence. The judge urged the prosecution to trim down the list of witnesses it intends to present, stressing the need to conclude the case as soon as possible. Defense lawyer Peter Haynes also raised the issue of disclosure, describing the situation as a “mess” due to the bulk of documents provided by the prosecution. Korner directed the parties to submit their positions in writing, saying the matters will be resolved either in writing or during the next status conference. Situation in the Republic of the Philippines The Prosecutor v. Rodrigo Roa Duterte ICC-01/21-01/25 Updated: February 2026 Suspected of the crimes against humanity of murder and attempted murder, allegedly committed in the Republic of the Philippines between 1 November 2011 and 16 March 2019. Surrendered to the custody of the International Criminal Court (ICC) on 12 March 2025. Confirmation of charges hearing to open on 23 February 2026. Date of birth: 28 March 1945 Nationality: national of the Republic of the Philippines Function(s) at the time of the alleged crimes: President of the Philippines, Mayor of Davao City, Vice Mayor of Davao City, and allegedly the founder and head of the Davao Death Squad (‘DDS’). Arrest warrant: issued on 7 March 2025 Surrender to ICC Custody: 12 March 2025 Initial appearance: 14 March 2025 Confirmation of charges hearing: scheduled on 23-27 February 2026 According to the Prosecution’s submission of the Document Containing the Charges, Mr Duterte is suspected of 3 counts of crimes against humanity allegedly committed from at least 1 November 2011 to 16 March 2019 in the Philippines: Key judicial developments OPENING OF THE INVESTIGATION On 24 May 2021, the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICC (“the Prosecution”) requested authorisation from the Chamber to initiate an investigation into crimes allegedly committed on the territory of the Philippines in the context of the “war on drugs” campaign waged by the Government of the Philippines between 1 November 2011 and 16 March 2019. On 14 June 2021, the Prosecution’s request was made public. On 15 September 2021, Pre-Trial Chamber I authorised the investigation. On 18 July 2023, following the Philippine authorities’ request for deferral and the subsequent temporary suspension of the investigative activities, the ICC Appeals Chamber delivered its judgment which confirmed the Chamber’s decision granting authorisation to the Prosecution to resume the investigation in relation to the situation in the Philippines. The Philippines, an ICC State Party since 1 November 2011, deposited a written notification of withdrawal from the Statute on 17 March 2018. Under article 127 of the Statute, that withdrawal took effect on 17 March 2019. Nevertheless, the ICC retains jurisdiction over crimes allegedly committed in the Philippines while the country was a State Party to the Statute. On 10 February 2025, the Prosecution applied for an arrest warrant against Mr Duterte for the crimes against humanity of murder, torture and rape. Having assessed the material submitted by the Prosecution, Pre-Trial Chamber I found reasonable grounds to believe that Mr Duterte is individually responsible as an indirect co-perpetrator for the crime against humanity of murder, allegedly committed in the Philippines between 1 November 2011 and 16 March 2019. The warrant of arrest against Mr Duterte was issued by the Chamber as “Secret” on 7 March 2025 and reclassified as “Public” on 11 March 2025. On 12 March 2025, Mr Duterte was surrendered to the International Criminal Court, after being arrested by the authorities of the Republic of the Philippines in accordance with the warrant of arrest issued by Pre-Trial Chamber I. He is currently in ICC custody. The initial appearance of Mr Duterte took place on 14 March 2025 before Pre-Trial Chamber I. Mr Duterte appeared in the hearing via video link from the ICC Detention Centre, as authorised by the Chamber. The Chamber verified the identity of the suspect and ensured that he was clearly informed of the crimes he is alleged to have committed and of his rights under the Rome Statute of the ICC in a language he fully understands and speaks. On 8 September 2025, Pre-Trial Chamber I postponed the commencement of the confirmation hearing in the case, which had been initially scheduled to start on 23 September 2025. Following a request from the Defence of Mr Duterte for an indefinite adjournment of the proceedings alleging that Mr Duterte is not fit to stand trial, the majority of the Chamber considered that a limited postponement of the hearing on the confirmation of charges was warranted to allow sufficient time to adjudicate the request and related matters. On 26 January 2026, Pre-Trial Chamber I found Mr Rodrigo Roa Duterte fit to take part in the pre-trial proceedings and rejected the Defence’s request for an indefinite adjournment. Having regard to the relevant legal principles, the medical assessment of a panel of three independent medical experts and all of the relevant circumstances of the case, the Chamber was satisfied that Mr Duterte is able effectively to exercise his procedural rights and is therefore fit to take part in the pre-trial proceedings, which are thereby resumed. The Chamber has scheduled the confirmation of charges hearing for 23 to 27 February 2026. The purpose of the confirmation of charges procedure is to determine whether there is sufficient evidence to establish substantial grounds to believe that the person committed the crimes he or she is suspected of. If the charges are confirmed, totally or partly, the case will be transferred to a Trial Chamber, which will conduct the subsequent phase of the proceedings: the trial. The Chamber will issue its decision on the confirmation of charges within 60 days after the confirmation hearing. The judges have allowed victims to participate in the proceedings. In this case, the judges appointed Joel Butuyan and Gilbert Andres, as well as Paolina Massidda of the Office of the Public Counsel for Victims (OPCV) as a single team of common legal representatives for any admitted victims. output.text: Ellen Tordesillas is president of VERA Files. A veteran reporter, she is the 1998 Marshall McLuhan fellow. Ellen Tordesillas is president of VERA Files. A veteran reporter, she is the 1998 Marshall McLuhan fellow. The newly-formed Trial Chamber III of the International Criminal Court ordered on May 1 parties concerned in the trial of former president Rodrigo Duterte to submit observations on his situation at the Scheveningen prison in The Hague, Netherlands as required by the Court’s rules and regulations. “The Chamber observes that, pursuant to the statutory framework, the Accused’s pre-trial detention shall be reviewed at least every 120 days. In light of the developments following the annual hearing, the Chamber considers it necessary to give the parties and participants the opportunity to submit any observations they may have regarding the Accused’s continued detention or release, with or without conditions, including the existence of any changed circumstances,” the order, signed by Presiding Judge Joanna Korner and the two other members of the chamber, Keebong Paek and Nicolas Guillou, stated. Duterte, facing charges of crimes against humanity in connection with his war on drugs campaign between 1 November 2011 and 16 March 2019 has been in detention since March 12, 2025. He was arrested in the Philippines on March 11, 2025 on the strength of a March 7, 2025 warrant issued by the ICC and surrendered to the Court upon arrival in The Hague. Duterte’s only appearance while in detention took place on 14 March 2025 via video link. He has waived his right to appear in subsequent court proceedings. Despite claims by Duterte’s counsel Nicholas Kaufman that his 81-year old client is “enfeebled”, the Pre-Trial Chamber I reviewed his health and detention situation and found him fit to stand the confirmation proceedings that took place on Feb. 23 to 27. The findings were affirmed by the mandatory annual review which took place on Feb. 27. Preparation for Duterte’s trial has started after the Pre-Trial Chamber I unanimously confirmed all the charges comprised of three counts of crimes against humanity. Trial Chamber III has called for a First Status Conference among parties concerned on May 27 to decide, among other matters, the date of the trial; estimated number of witnesses to be called and number of hours of in-court testimony; use of expert witnesses; testimony given by audio or video link; estimated volume of documentary and other non-testimonial evidence to be relied upon at trial. output.title: A smiling Duterte appears in person for the first time before the ICC
output.description: Dressed in black suit and white polo shirt, Duterte appeared attentive as Trial Chamber III tackled procedural and administrative issues ahead of his Nov. 30 trial on crimes against humanity.
output.text: A smiling Rodrigo Duterte sat through more than an hour of proceedings at the International Criminal Court on Wednesday, marking the former president’s first in-person appearance before the tribunal since his arrest in March 2025. Dressed in black suit and white polo shirt, Duterte appeared attentive as Trial Chamber III tackled procedural and administrative issues ahead of his Nov. 30 trial on crimes against humanity. Photographs released after the hearing showed Duterte walking without a wheelchair and without eyeglasses. He appeared thinner and sported a grayish stubble beard, with thick, dark brown hair noticeably different from his usual style before his arrest, prompting speculations that he may have been wearing a wig. The appearance was Duterte’s first before the ICC in person since March 14, 2025, when he joined his initial hearing before the Pre-Trial Chamber I by video link from detention. output.title: ICC Trial Chamber orders submissions on Rodrigo Duterte detention review
output.description: The International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III has directed concerned parties to submit their observations on the continued detention of former president Rodrigo Duterte by May 8, following the confirmation of charges against him.
output.text:
The International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III has directed concerned parties to submit their observations on the continued detention of former president Rodrigo Duterte by May 8, following the confirmation of charges against him.

In an order dated May 1, the Chamber identified the parties as the Office of the Prosecutor, Duterte’s defense counsel, the Legal Representatives of the Victims, and the Office of the Public Counsel for Victims.

“The Chamber observes that, pursuant to the statutory framework, the Accused’s pre-trial detention shall be reviewed at least every 120 days,” the ICC said.

“In light of the developments following the annual hearing, the Chamber considers it necessary to give the parties and participants the opportunity to submit any observations they may have regarding the Accused’s continued detention or release, with or without conditions, including the existence of any changed circumstances,” it added.

Trial Chamber III is set to hold a status conference on May 27 on the crimes against humanity charges linked to Duterte’s war on illegal drugs.

The proceedings will be streamed on the ICC website with a 30-minute delay.

On April 23, the ICC confirmed charges of crimes against humanity against the 81-year-old Duterte.

The confirmed charges are:

  • Count 1: Murder as a crime against humanity in Davao City during his mayoral tenure, involving at least 19 victims between 2013 and around June 2016, through indirect co-perpetration, ordering and/or inducing, and/or aiding and abetting;
  • Count 2: Murder as a crime against humanity of “high-value targets” across the Philippines during his presidency, involving at least 14 victims between around July 2016 and July 2017, through indirect co-perpetration and/or ordering, inducing, or aiding and abetting; and
  • Count 3: Murder and attempted murder as crimes against humanity in barangay clearance operations nationwide, involving at least 45 victims (43 killed and two injured) between around July 2016 and September 2018, through indirect co-perpetration, ordering and/or inducing, and/or aiding and abetting.

Duterte’s camp has sought permission from the ICC to appeal the Pre-Trial Chamber I’s decision confirming the charges.

In a filing dated April 29, defense counsel Nicholas Kaufman said the impugned decision raised two appealable issues.

The first concerns whether the Pre-Trial Chamber erred by adopting a “flexible approach” and broadly defining the scope of the charges.

The second questions whether the Chamber erred in law by failing to provide a reasoned evidentiary basis for confirming the charges.

Earlier, Pre-Trial Chamber I denied Duterte’s request for interim release in 2025 and ordered his continued detention in January 2026.

In February, it held the annual review hearing on his detention, where parties and participants submitted their observations.

Duterte was arrested in the Philippines on March 11, 2025 and has since been detained at the ICC Detention Centre in Scheveningen, The Hague, Netherlands.—MCG GMA News

The Presidency also "DECIDES to refer the case of The Prosecutor v. Rodrigo Roa Duterte to Trial Chamber III;" formally transferring jurisdiction over the next phase of proceedings. It said the composition of the chamber was guided by the need to ensure "efficient management of the Court's workload," taking into account "the experience and expertise of each judge," as well as the need to expedite proceedings and balance judicial assignments. "CONSIDERING the current and anticipated overall judicial workload of the Court and the necessity to ensure sound management of the same, the need to expedite proceedings, the workload and individual concerns of the respective judges, particularly those assigned to the Trial Division, their previous involvement in cases, as well as the experience and expertise of each judge," the decision stated. With the chamber now in place, the case formally enters the trial stage, where judges will oversee proceedings, rule on evidence, and ultimately determine guilt or innocence. "At trial, the Defence will prove that the aforementioned 'State policy' is a complete fiction. The Defence will also show that the evidence of very same criminal witnesses, so gleefully peddled by the former President's many detractors, has zero weight," he added. MANILA -- The International Criminal Court on Tuesday announced that it has constituted the Trial Chamber in the case against former President Rodrigo Duterte. This moves the proceedings to the trial phase, after Pre-Trial Chamber I confirmed all three counts of crimes against humanity against him on April 23. READ: Duterte to face ICC trial after judges confirm charges Here is the information about the three judges of the newly constituted Trial Chamber III available on the ICC website. Joanna Korner (United Kingdom) Courtesy: International Criminal Court Korner, a veteran British jurist, brings more than 45 years of experience in criminal law as both a judge and barrister. She has served as a judge of the Crown Court of England and Wales since 2012, handling complex cases including fraud and murder. A Queen’s Counsel since 1993, she also served for eight years as a senior prosecutor at the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, where she led several high-profile war crimes prosecutions. At the ICC, she is assigned to the Trial Division and has presided over proceedings including The Prosecutor v. Ali Muhammad Ali Abd-Al-Rahman (“Ali Kushayb”). Keebong Paek (Republic of Korea) Courtesy: International Criminal Court Paek, elected to the ICC in 2023, has more than three decades of experience as a prosecutor and legal expert. He began his career in 1992 and handled a wide range of criminal cases. He has also served internationally, including as a senior adviser at the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, with expertise in transnational crime, terrorism, and international cooperation. He was also responsible for drafting the implementation bill for Korea's ratification of the Rome Statute, and representing the country at ICC Preparatory Commission sessions and the Kampala Review Conference. Before joining the ICC, he was in private practice focusing on cross-border investigations and international criminal law. Nicolas Guillou (France) Courtesy: International Criminal Court Guillou, elected as judge of the ICC in 2023, previously served as a Pre-Trial Judge at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, and is currently handling cases involving war crimes and crimes against humanity. He has held senior roles in international justice, including as Chef de Cabinet to the President of the Special Tribunal for Lebanon, and as a Liaison Prosecutor at the U.S. Department of Justice. He began his career as an investigative judge in France and specializes in international and European criminal law. CONVICTION BY 2028? The ICC said Trial Chamber III will oversee all subsequent proceedings, including setting the timetable for trial and resolving preliminary issues such as disclosure of evidence and procedural matters. Victims’ lawyer Kristina Conti said families of alleged extrajudicial killing victims remain hopeful the case will move swiftly. “If the ICC keeps at this pace, victims are hopeful that trial can start as soon as this year, and perhaps the conviction of Duterte be had by 2028,” she told ABS-CBN News. Duterte, 81, will be the first Asian former head of state to face trial at the ICC, which prosecutes individuals for the world's worst crimes such as war crimes and crimes against humanity. Simon Wohlfahrt, AFP/File MANILA (3rd UPDATE) — Former president Rodrigo Duterte will face trial before the International Criminal Court after judges confirmed crimes against humanity charges tied to his war on drugs. The Hague-based tribunal said its ICC Pre-Trial Chamber I “unanimously confirmed all the charges” against Duterte and “committed him to trial”, based on arguments and evidence presented during 4-day hearings in February. It added that pre-trial judges concluded that "there are substantial grounds to believe that Mr. Duterte is responsible for the crimes against humanity of murder and attempted murder" between November 1, 2011 and March 16, 2019, covering Duterte’s time as Davao City mayor and later as president. “These crimes were committed as part of a widespread and systematic attack against a civilian population,” it added. The 81-year-old will be the first Asian former head of state to face trial at the ICC, which prosecutes individuals for the world's worst crimes such as war crimes and crimes against humanity. “Next steps: Upon the transfer of the case to a Trial Chamber, the Trial Chamber will decide on the next steps. Trials at the ICC are fair and impartial, and the Defence will have sufficient time to prepare its case, while respecting the rights of victims,” the ICC said. Kaufman: ICC jurisdiction decision on ‘big catch’ Duterte was expected DEFENSE: CREDIBILITY OF WITNESSES NOT ASSESSED In a statement, Duterte's lead counsel Nicholas Kaufman argued that the credibility of the witnesses was "never assessed at confirmation." "The Pre Trial Chamber found that the crucial word ‘neutralize’, used to define a so-called State or organizational policy, was understood by those involved in the operations to mean to ‘kill’. This is hardly surprising when the whole of the Prosecution’s case, as pasted into the concluding paragraphs of the Pre-Trial Chamber’s decision, is based on the uncorroborated statements of vicious self-confessed murderers acting as cooperating witnesses," he said. "At trial, the Defence will prove that the aforementioned 'State policy' is a complete fiction. The Defense will also show that the evidence of very same criminal witnesses, so gleefully peddled by the former President’s many detractors, has zero weight," he added. MALACAÑANG RESPECTS ICC DECISION Malacañang said it "respects" the ICC decision. “Hustisya ang kailangan[g] makuha sa mga kasong ito,” Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said in a statement. “Parehong partido ang makikinabang rito. Hustisya para sa akusado kung walang sala o hustisya rin sa mga biktima kung naabuso naman ang kanilang karapatan,” she said. 'VERY GOOD NEWS' Duterte Panagutin Campaign Network convenor Jojo Lacanilao described the development as “very good news,” noting that recent legal efforts opposing the ICC process appeared to be losing traction. “Very good news kasi two days in a row, mukhang hindi effective ang Invictus, na tinatawag nila. So happy about this justice moves on, hinihintay namin ang pag tingkad ng araw ng hustisya na makakamit natin pagdating ng trial at maconvict na ang dating president,” Lacanilao said. He expressed gratitude on behalf of the families of extrajudicial killing (EJK) victims, many of whom, he said, remained fearful but were beginning to find the courage to come forward. “Kami ay natutuwa at nagpapasalamat para sa mga biktima ng EJK. Malaki pa ang takot nila pero ngayon kahit konti nagkakaroon nasila ng lakas na loob na harapin ang lahat ng ito. We are very happy with this development starting with kahapon sa jurisdiction issue ngayon nilabas agad ang confirmation of charges parang feeling ko tuloy tuloy na ito so maraming salamat sa mga sumusuporta po,” he said. Lacanilao said efforts were ongoing to identify additional victims who could submit evidence to the court. “Things are looking good hopefully magko-consolidate pa rin ang mga victims at tutulong pa rin kayo sa paglabas ng hustisya at makamit na nating lahat ito,” he said. TRIAL APPEARANCE The announcement comes a day after the ICC threw out a challenge against its jurisdiction by Duterte's defense team. It is unclear whether Duterte will attend his trial. His defense team says he is too weak mentally to follow proceedings and he did not appear at Wednesday’s reading of the decision. The only time he has been seen since his arrest and transfer to The Hague was at an initial appearance via videolink in March 2025. The Rome Statute, however, requires the presence of the accused during trial. Under the Rome Statute, the Trial Chamber "may remove the accused and shall make provision for him or her to observe the trial and instruct counsel from outside the courtroom, through the use of communications technology" in case they disrupt the trial.That provision will be temporary and "shall be taken only in exceptional circumstances after other reasonable alternatives have proved inadequate." Rome Statute requires Duterte's presence at ICC trial Duterte's looming trial comes as the court faces the most difficult time in its 24-year history, with the United States sanctioning key judges and officials after the ICC issued arrest warrants for Israel's leader over the Gaza war. — With reports from Harlene Delgado and Lyza Aquino, ABS-CBN News Now comes the exciting part. A total of 539 relatives of extrajudicial killings in the Duterte drug war have applied as “participating victims” in the upcoming trial of ex-president Rodrigo Duterte in the International Criminal Court. Atty Maria Kristina Conti, ICC Assistant to Counsel and secretary general of NUPL-NCR, said the participating victims will be consulted periodically for their views and concerns about the trial but are not expected to show up in court and testify vs the ex-president. Participating victims are separate from the actual witnesses who will testify against Duterte after being screened by the Prosecutor and Defense. Conti noted not all of the victims in the drug war will be included in the case because of the limited scope of the investigation, saying the trial will only tackle cases from November 2011 to March 2019. She said that under the Rome Statute, Duterte must be present during the trial, saying some accused in previous ICC trials did not return after being granted interim release. Rome Statute requires Duterte's presence at ICC trial She said she expects the ICC to "bend over backwards" to accommodate Duterte, saying the Hague-based tribunal may allow Duterte to join the proceedings via video call or even allow him to turn his camera off. “Kung hindi ka makaupo, sige nakahiga ka. She said Duterte’s trial may start as early as October this year, adding that she expects the hearing to start within the year. The ICC earlier upheld its jurisdiction over the crimes against humanity case filed against Duterte after the tribunal’s Appeals Chamber on Wednesday junked petitions to halt proceedings against the Philippines’ 16th president. The decision affirms the ICC Pre-Trial Chamber’s October 2025 ruling that the court has authority over the case, contrary to Duterte's lead defense counsel Nicholas Kaufman’s assertions that the Philippines was no longer a part of the ICC when the Pre-Trial Chamber authorized the opening of an investigation in September 2021. Gilbert Andres, among the lawyers for extrajudicial killing victims, on Saturday said the International Criminal Court prosecution is prepared to prove the credibility of its witnesses against former President Rodrigo Duterte, rejecting claims by defense lawyer Nicholas Kaufman that prosecution witnesses are merely “liars.” Andres, counsel for EJK victims before the ICC, said it is the duty of the Office of the Prosecutor to “prove, give evidence beyond reasonable doubt” to secure Duterte’s conviction. He also dismissed Kaufman’s claim that Pre-Trial Chamber I’s decision was merely an “accommodation” for the prosecution, stressing that the chamber had sufficient legal basis for its ruling. Kaufman to appeal ICC chamber’s confirmation of charges against Duterte According to Andres, the confirmation of charges only requires “substantial grounds to believe” and not proof beyond reasonable doubt. “Kung ano man ang mga argumento tungkol sa credibility ng witness hindi po ‘yan sa Pre-Trial Chamber, ‘yan ay sa trial proper,” said Andres. “Nagkaroon ng proseso doon sa confirmation of the charges… So, talagang nirespeto ang right to fair trial nung suspek.” He mentioned that the hearing was originally scheduled for September 23, 2025, but was only opened on February 23 this year, showing that the defense was given ample opportunity. The conference, scheduled to start 10:30 a.m. in The Hague (4:30 p.m. in Manila), will be livestreamed online with a 30-minute delay. It will tackle details of the prosecution’s case, including its list of witnesses and evidence, the number of hours to be given to the prosecutor, the ongoing disclosure to the defense and other possible incidents to be added in the case. The parties will also discuss the trial schedule, which will start on Nov. 30, including the proposal to have “blocks of hearings with breaks.” It remains unclear if Duterte will be present as he was previously allowed to skip the pre-trial proceedings. But during the last status conference on June 23, presiding judge Joanna Korner said they expect Duterte to attend the September status conference “unless there’s some medical issue” that would prevent him from doing so. Duterte has never appeared in person before ICC judges. He was last seen by the public on March 14, 2025, when he appeared via video link during his initial appearance hearing before the ICC Pre-Trial Chamber I. His family and lawyers regularly visit him in his detention facility in The Hague. Philstar.com is one of the most vibrant, opinionated, discerning communities of readers on cyberspace.
