output.text: A man holds a portrait of former Philippines president Rodrigo Duterte in front of the International Criminal Court (ICC) where he will be appearing, in The Hague on March 14, 2025. Nicolas Tucat, AFP/File MANILA -- The International Criminal Court (ICC) has allowed prosecutors to examine some materials taken from former president Rodrigo Roa Duterte following his arrest, while rejecting a separate request for access to all keys found among his belongings. The rulings, originally issued on May 28 and June 22 but released to the public in redacted form on Friday, showed that Trial Chamber III partly granted the prosecution's requests for materials kept by the ICC Registry in connection with its investigation into Duterte's alleged crimes against humanity. In its May 28 decision, the chamber granted the prosecution's request to inspect certain redacted materials recovered from Duterte's belongings after he was surrendered to the custody of the Court on March 12, 2025. The judges said there were reasonable grounds to believe the requested examination could produce evidence necessary for the investigation and found the request "necessary and proportionate" to the prosecution's investigative needs. The chamber also ordered prosecutors to submit, within one month after receiving the materials, a report detailing the measures taken to protect Duterte's private information. The judges, however, criticized the prosecution for waiting more than a year after being informed of the Registry's report before seeking access to the materials. "The Chamber deplores the fact that the Prosecution did not make this request at an earlier stage of the proceedings and provides no reason for this failure," the decision said. The chamber also granted prosecutors access to the Registry's inventory of items obtained from Duterte upon his arrest by ordering the reclassification of confidential Registry documents. However, it said it was premature to rule on prosecutors' request to access additional materials until after they had reviewed the inventory. The Court likewise granted the prosecution's request to preserve the value of any money found among Duterte's belongings, ordering the Registry to take appropriate measures to prevent its devaluation. The chamber said the funds could be subject to forfeiture or used for possible reparations to victims if Duterte is eventually convicted. In a separate decision dated June 22, the chamber partly granted a second prosecution request seeking additional materials from the Registry after prosecutors reviewed the inventory. The judges approved access to two categories of redacted materials, saying they could produce evidence necessary for the investigation and that the examination was proportionate to the prosecution's needs. However, the chamber denied the prosecution's request for access to all keys in the Registry's custody, saying they failed to explain what the keys were for or how they could provide relevant evidence. The judges also noted the defense's argument that some keys may belong to Duterte's relatives, making access to them a possible intrusion into the privacy rights of third parties. "The requested access to the Keys is neither necessary nor proportionate, and should therefore be rejected," the chamber said. The chamber also ordered prosecutors to file any additional requests for access to materials in the Registry's custody by June 30, noting the prosecution's earlier delays in seeking the evidence. Duterte's defense had previously opposed what it described as the prosecution's "evidence hunt" and asked the chamber to impose a deadline for any further requests for materials held by the Registry. READ: Duterte defense slams ICC prosecution's 'evidence hunt', demands strict deadline These evidentiary developments unfold as Trial Chamber III maps out the critical roadmap leading to Duterte's trial, which is scheduled to begin on November 30. Presiding Judge Joanna Korner has signaled that the former president is expected to personally attend an important status conference scheduled for September 7, unless restricted by a medical issue. READ: ICC judge expects Duterte to attend Sept. 7 status conference The chamber notes that this specific hearing will be pivotal, occurring immediately after the court receives the prosecution's trial brief, witness lists, and an independent expert medical evaluation of Duterte's health due in mid-to-late August. Duterte currently faces three counts of crimes against humanity for murder and attempted murder at the ICC, stemming from his controversial anti-drug campaign between 2011 and 2019 during his tenures as mayor of Davao City and president of the Philippines. READ: Amid high public interest, ICC judge issues warning to counsels vs. media statements The International Criminal Court in The Hague, The Netherlands MANILA — The defense team of former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte has pushed back against the International Criminal Court (ICC) Prosecution's latest request to inspect items seized during his arrest, labeling their efforts a late-stage "fishing expedition". In two separate public redacted responses submitted to ICC Trial Chamber III on June 26, 2026, lead defense counsel Peter Haynes, asked the court to reject multiple investigative requests from the prosecution to prevent undue delays in the high-profile case. 'FAR TOO LATE' REQUESTS In the first filing, labeled "Response to Prosecution’s request for materials in the custody of the Registry," the defense argued that the prosecution's request to inspect materials currently held by the ICC Registry comes far too late in the procedural timeline. Haynes noted that the prosecution has known about the items in the Registry's possession since March 14, 2025, but failed to seek possession until well after the confirmation of charges. "Such requests are usually made within days of the arrival of the suspect in custody, or at the earliest opportunity," the defense stated. Haynes warned that launching an expansive new analysis of the evidence at this point threatens the prosecution's own stated timeline to complete case disclosures by September 30, 2026. The defense also dismissed the prosecution’s demands for a new inventory and a court order to freeze any money found among the seized items. Haynes argued that an existing "chain of custody" form already functions as a proper inventory and that any seized funds are already securely held by the Registry, making a new freezing order entirely redundant. Amid high public interest, ICC judge issues warning to counsels vs. media statements 'FISHING EXPEDITION' The legal battle intensified in the second response, found in "Response to Prosecution’s Second Request for Materials in the Custody of the Registry,” which addressed a subsequent prosecution motion filed on June 9, 2026, seeking access to specific redacted items and "all keys in the Registry's custody". While the defense noted it "does not oppose access" to certain redacted materials, it drew a hard line against handing over the keys. Haynes slammed the request as lacking basic legal justification, arguing that investigators have failed to connect the keys to the alleged crimes. "The request is, in substance, a fishing expedition," the defense asserted. "The Prosecution cannot be permitted to examine the keys in order to articulate, post facto, the evidential foundation required to justify that examination in the first place." The defense also raised significant privacy concerns for third parties, noting that the keys were seized while Duterte was traveling with his family. "It is entirely possible that the keys provide access to material belonging to, or concerning, his relatives, such that their examination would intrude upon the privacy rights of third parties," Haynes argued, stating that the move is neither necessary nor proportionate. DEFENSE DEMANDS STRICT DEADLINE To prevent the trial from being derailed by ongoing evidence hunts, the defense has formally requested Trial Chamber III—led by Presiding Judge Joanna Korner, Judge Keebong Paek, and Judge Nicolas Guillou—to enforce a strict deadline of June 30 for any further prosecution requests regarding Registry materials. Haynes emphasized that enforcing a strict deadline is crucial to ensuring the defense has adequate time to prepare its strategy and to safeguard the "expeditiousness of the proceedings. The dispute stems from a series of motions that began on May 1, when the ICC Prosecution first filed a request for the Registry to produce a full inventory of items seized from Duterte upon his arrest, grant full access to investigative materials, and freeze any seized monetary assets. Following formal observations submitted by both the Duterte defense team and the Registry, Trial Chamber III issued a partial ruling on May 28. In that decision, the Chamber granted the prosecution’s request to freeze the seized money and ordered the Registry to generate an official inventory. However, the judges ruled it "premature" to grant the prosecution blanket access to the items at that time, directing the investigators to file a separate, more specific request if they wished to inspect any particular item listed on the newly generated inventory. This directive led to the prosecution's subsequent June 9 motion targeting specific redacted materials and all keys in custody, which the defense is now vigorously fighting. ICC judge expects Duterte to attend Sept. 7 status conference RELATED VIDEO: ABS-CBN News MANILA — Exactly a decade since “Project Double Barrel” — the code name for the drug war launched by former President Rodrigo Duterte that left more than 6,000 "drug personalities" dead in law enforcement operations — families of victims of extrajudicial killings joined artists, journalists, academics, lawyers, church groups, and human rights defenders to launch Dekada ng Sama-samang Pag-alala, Pagkakaisa para sa Hustisya (A Decade of Collective Remembrance, Unity for Justice). The launch at Bantayog ng mga Bayani in Quezon City featured a solemn candle-lighting ceremony led by surviving families of the drug war. Human rights groups, faith-based communities, and legal organizations stood alongside them, underscoring a shared demand for accountability. ICC judge expects Duterte to attend Sept. 7 status conference Organizers drew a stark historical parallel, likening July 1, 2016, to September 21, 1972, when Proclamation 1081 institutionalized Martial Law. “July 1 stands as the foundational date of a decade of state-sanctioned violence and impunity,” the coalition declared. “This day signals 10 years of grief, mourning, resistance, and most importantly, the journey from family-victims to survivors.” The program opened with a performance by documentary theater group RESBAK (RESpond and Break the Silence Against the Killings), dramatizing the lived experiences of victims’ families. The event also welcomed the journalist and author of Some People Need Killing, who visited to stand in solidarity with survivors. Fr. Flavie Villanueva, known for his ministry to EJK victims, led a prayer marking the anniversary, calling for justice. The coalition emphasized its principle: “Every Filipino deserves due process. That was never negotiable.” It urged the public to reflect on “the voices, time, dignity, and futures that were taken — and on our collective responsibility to uphold due process, accountability, and human worth.” Amid high public interest, ICC judge issues warning to counsels vs. media statements The National Council of Churches in the Philippines (NCCP) issued a searing statement, marking the day Duterte became president. “Then the slaughter started. The so-called war on drugs made killings of thousands of suspected drug users and small-time pushers, many from poor and marginalized communities," it said. "Many lost their lives without due process. Behind the statistics are grieving parents, widows, orphaned children, and communities left to bear the enduring trauma of violence.” The NCCP condemned the culture of impunity fostered by Duterte and his allies, adding that abuses extended to activists and human rights defenders through the National Task Force to End Local Communist Armed Conflict. The church group welcomed the ICC’s arrest of Duterte for crimes against humanity but warned that “his co-accused, including the fugitive Sen. Bato, remains at large.” It also noted that killings continue under President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., citing more than 1,200 drug-related deaths documented by the Dahas Project. ICC Registry sets digital workflow, redaction rules for Duterte trial “Such is the legacy of the Duterte presidency,” the NCCP declared. “Ten years after the beginning of the so-called ‘war on drugs,’ our vigil continues. We will continue to stand with the bereaved, defend the oppressed, and proclaim that every human life is sacred because every person bears the image of God.” The coalition’s DEKADA program will run until December 2026, featuring exhibitions, film screenings, discussions, and public interventions both online and in-person. Organizers said the initiative is meant to move beyond narratives of violence and spectacle, centering instead on the humanity of those affected. “Grounded in remembrance, we hold steadfast to justice — because the fight for accountability is the fight for our nation’s future,” the coalition declared. U.S. President Donald Trump listens to members of his Cabinet speak during a meeting in the Cabinet Room of the White House on May 27, 2026 in Washington, DC. Win McNamee/Getty Images/AFP/File Three International Criminal Court judges sanctioned by the United States filed a lawsuit Wednesday against President Donald Trump and other senior US officials, arguing the measures against them are unlawful. In a New York court filing, judges Kimberly Prost of Canada, Solomy Balungi Bossa of Uganda and Reine Adelaide Sophie Alapini-Gansou of Benin alleged the sanctions aimed to "exert extra-judicial pressure." ICC judge in Duterte case among those sanctioned by Trump admin over Israel, US cases The Trump administration has imposed sanctions on at least 11 ICC officials, including the chief prosecutor, which consist of travel bans and asset freezes. Many of the measures have been direct reprisals for investigations into key US ally Israel by the ICC, which in 2024 issued an arrest warrant for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for alleged war crimes. EXPLAINER: How does the International Criminal Court work? Wednesday's lawsuit said the sanctions imposed on Prost, Bossa and Alapini-Gansou were aimed at "punishing them for prior judicial decisions and coercing them into prioritizing their private interests over deciding cases on the basis of the law and facts." It added that the measures were "tantamount to the financial death penalty," as the judges are unable to use credit cards, access banking services and use online platforms like Amazon and Google. "The imposition of such draconian sanctions on international judges is unprecedented," said the 66-page filing, which demands the sanctions be lifted. Alongside Trump, the lawsuit names Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, and Bradley Smith, director of the Office of Foreign Assets Control. The United States, Israel and Russia are among the countries that reject the ICC, which is backed by nearly all Western democracies. The ICC was set up in 2002 as a court of last resort when countries do not have adequate legal systems to ensure accountability. During Trump's first term, the United States also took action against the top ICC prosecutor in a successful attempt to block an investigation into alleged abuses during the US-led war in Afghanistan. Former president Joe Biden's administration lifted the sanctions and sought limited cooperation with the court, especially over Ukraine. ICC chief prosecutor Karim Khan suspended amid sex abuse claims ICC judge expects Duterte to attend Sept. 7 status conference RELATED VIDEOS: Rodrigo Duterte’s initial appearance on 14 March 2025 before Pre-Trial Chamber I of the International Criminal Court. Handout MANILA — The International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III on Tuesday signaled that former president Rodrigo Duterte is expected to personally attend the September 7 status conference in his crimes against humanity case. During the second status conference on Tuesday, Presiding Judge Joanna Korner noted that Duterte's absence was allowed only because the hearing was expected to be brief. "Again Mr. Haynes, we've excused your client's attendance today but as I think we made clear, it's only because it's a relatively short hearing," Korner told defense lawyer Peter Haynes. Haynes acknowledged the chamber's expectation that Duterte would appear in future proceedings. "I was going to observe of course that the movement of a detainee from the detention unit to the court is an unsettling experience even for the sturdiest of clients. But he's fully aware that you will expect to see him sooner rather than later," Haynes said. Near the end of the hearing, the chamber set tentative dates for future status conferences on July 14, September 7, October 13 and November 2. Korner said the scheduled conferences could be canceled if there were no matters requiring discussion. "These are all dates that we put into the calendar but if it turns out there's no need for anything to be discussed then we may vacate them. But otherwise it's 7th of September, 13th of October and then the 2nd of November," she said. Duterte's ICC trial to start November 30 The judge, however, singled out the September 7 conference as particularly significant because it would take place after the Chamber receives all required submissions from all the parties involved, including the prosecution trial brief and experts report concerning Duterte's medical condition. "I rather feel the one on the 7th of September because by the time we've had the reports is likely to be an important one and for that certainly Mr. Haynes we would expect Mr. Duterte to be here unless there's some medical issue," Korner said. Under the schedule discussed during Tuesday's hearing, the medical expert's report on Duterte's evaluation is due on August 18, while the Registry is expected to file the report on August 24. ICC Registry says Duterte’s falls were ‘rare occasions,’ disputes defense claim of ‘frequent episodes’ Parties and participants initially have until August 31 to submit their observations. However, prosecutors sought an additional week to file observations on the medical report, citing a heavy workload linked to other pre-trial deadlines. Prosecutor Julian Nichols told the chamber that the prosecution would also have to submit its trial brief, witness list, evidence list and complete disclosure requirements by August 31. "What we're asking for is one more week to file our observations," Nichols said, adding that the prosecution expected to be "extremely busy" during the final week of August. The defense and the common legal representatives of victims did not oppose the request. "You can have the extra week," Korner ruled. The chamber also addressed organizational matters involving the common legal representatives of victims, approved arrangements for the handling of confidential information, and heard the prosecution's request to expand the page limit of its trial brief from 120 to 160 pages. Before adjourning, Korner delivered a reminder regarding public comments about the case, noting the intense media attention surrounding the proceedings. "This case has attracted, not surprisingly, a substantial amount of media interest in the Philippines in particular," she said. Amid high public interest, ICC judge issues warning to counsels vs. media statements Korner emphasized "the need for the media to report to the public accurately and fairly what is said in court and above all to avoid speculation." She reminded journalists that "anything which is said in private session may not be reported." The judge further criticized public comments made by defense counsel Nicholas Kaufman following appellate rulings in the case, saying some remarks were "wholly inappropriate." "We see no reason why counsel should feel it necessary to make any comment to the media. The appropriate forum for counsel to raise matters is in the courtroom. Trials are not conducted by the court of public opinion but by this court during the course of the proceedings," Korner said. Duterte faces three counts of crimes against humanity for murder and attempted murder before the ICC in connection with killings linked to his anti-drug campaign between 2011 to 2019, as mayor of Davao City and as president of the Philippines. Rome Statute requires Duterte's presence at ICC trial DILG, PNP say no formal communication on alleged ICC warrants vs. Go, ex-cops 'Invictus': Rodrigo Duterte summarizes condition before ICC hearing A person stands by two life-size cardboard cutouts of former Philippines' president Rodrigo Duterte during a demonstration in his support outside the International Criminal Court (ICC) where he will be questioned on charges of crimes against humanity, in The Hague on February 23, 2026. Simon Wohlfahrt, AFP/File MANILA -- International Criminal Court Trial Chamber III presiding judge Joanna Korner on Tuesday issued a warning to the counsels involved in the case of former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte against giving statements to the media amid the high public interest in the case. During Tuesday’s second status conference, Korner warned the defense, prosecution, and victims' counsels not only to be courteous and respectful to the Chamber, but also to be careful in giving statements to the media. READ: ICC sets agenda for 2nd Duterte status conference READ: ICC sets rules and timelines for Rodrigo Duterte trial Korner cited an incident involving former defense counsel Nicholas Kaufman, who commented to the media on the decision of the ICC Appeals Chamber on the issue of jurisdiction, despite being previously warned by the Chamber. “Regrettably, that reminder had no effect. On the 26th of April of this year, after the Appeals Chamber had made its decision on jurisdiction, Kaufman gave at least two interviews commenting on the decision. Some of those comments were his personal view of legal decisions made by the Court as a whole, and were on any showing, wholly inappropriate, moreso when made by a counsel in a case,” she said. “In light of this previous history, this Trial Chamber feels it incumbent to repeat the reminder, or warning, to all counsel in the case, for the reasons that I have already expressed as to the importance of this trial,” Korner added. Korner likewise reminded counsels that any concerns should be raised in court, and not through the media. “We see no reason why counsel should feel it necessary to make any comment to the media. The appropriate form for counsel to raise matters is in the court room. Trials are not conducted by the court of public opinion but by this court during the course of the proceedings,” she said. In a statement, Kaufman said that his actions did not violate "counsel's ethical obligations at the ICC." "She [Judge Korner] has clearly studied the code of conduct for ICC counsel closely - with me in mind - but found nothing that I offended other than judicial sensitivity," he added. "As she is presumably aware, nothing that I said is at variance with what is currently being said in corridors and elsewhere," Kaufman added. "And if the media cannot benefit from the honest and raw views of defence counsel then all that remains is the Prosecution’s narrative." Kaufman withdrew as Duterte's legal counsel on May 8, a move that was approved by the ICC three days later. "The former President was proud to have me as his counsel and the arguments raised at confirmation will be those, God willing, that I hope will lead to his ultimate acquittal," said Kaufman. REMINDER TO MEDIA Korner also gave a reminder to the media to ensure that it is accurately and fairly reporting the proceedings, and to avoid any speculation. “This case has attracted, not surprisingly, a substantial amount of media interest in the Philippines in particular. That’s not, of course, only mainstream media, but, as is common these days, social media, and additionally, appears to have provoked suppliers of what is undoubtedly fake news, and obviously fake news,” she said. “The first thing we need to emphasize is the need for the media to report to the public accurately and fairly what is said in court. And above all, to avoid speculation. That is important in any trial, and doubly important when it comes to a trial of serious allegations. Nothing can be more serious than this of criminal activity,” Korner added. The Chamber ended the second status conference in less than 30 minutes, after they discussed deadlines and other matters related to the case. The status conference also discussed the deadline for submitting observations on the report of medical experts on the health of former President Duterte. The prosecution asked for a one-week extension from August 31. Also discussed was how the protocol for handling confidential information, and the number of pages of the prosecution's Trial Brief which is estimated to be up to 160 pages. Duterte had submitted a waiver of personal appearance to attend the status conference. He had also instructed his lawyers to deal with the procedural matters listed on the status conference agenda, as well as any other matters that may be discussed during the hearing. The next status conferences will be held on July 14, September 7, October 3 and November 2. The ICC Pre-Trial Chamber I officially confirmed the charges against Duterte on April 23, 2026, leading to the rapid constitution of Trial Chamber III by the ICC Presidency on April 28 to handle the absolute merits of the case. READ: Duterte's ICC trial to start November 30 Duterte is facing three charges of crimes against humanity for the murder of thousands of alleged drug users and peddlers in police operations during his tenure as Davao City Mayor and as Philippine President. The Philippines’ 16th President — who was arrested in Manila on March 2025 — is the first Asian to be hurled before the international tribunal. -- with a report from Jofelle Tesorio
